title: Your first Blyx program
summary: Run a greeting, change its text, and read what your program wrote.

sections.heading: Enter through main
sections.text: Every executable starts in a parameterless fn main(). The statements inside its braces run in order. A line beginning with // is a comment.

sections.heading: Write to the console
sections.text: println!(value) evaluates one expression and writes it followed by a newline. print!(value) writes without a newline. Use consecutive calls to print several values.

sections.heading: Try a change
sections.text: Replace the greeting with your name. Add a second println! that evaluates 6 * 7. The second line should read 42.

title: Install the compiler
summary: Choose an archive for your operating system and check the installed version.

sections.heading: Download blyxc
sections.text: The 0.2.0 release ships archives for Windows x86-64, Linux x86-64 and macOS Apple Silicon. Extract the archive and place the executable in a directory on PATH. With PowerShell you can also run .\blyxc.exe from the extracted directory.

sections.heading: Check your installation
sections.text: Run the version command. For the guide’s release the response is blyxc 0.2.0.

sections.heading: Install from source
sections.text: With Cargo and a host linker installed, select the release tag to reproduce this guide’s compiler.

sections.heading: Choose an execution path
sections.text: The downloaded CLI can interpret a .blyx file immediately. Install rustc and the host linker when you need blyxc build to produce an executable.

title: Values, bindings and scope
summary: Use immutable bindings, mutable state, and a block-local name.

sections.heading: Bind a value
sections.text: let creates an immutable binding. let mut allows assignment within the same value kind. Both forms need an initializer to execute.

sections.heading: Shadow a name
sections.text: A nested block can introduce its own binding with the same name. The example prints 8 from the inner block and 3 after the block ends.

sections.heading: Choose a numeric type
sections.text: Whole-number literals use checked signed 64-bit arithmetic during execution. Decimal literals such as 2.5 and 1e-2 use f64. true and false are booleans. Text is written in double quotes.

sections.heading: Try a change
sections.text: Replace the inner declaration with an assignment to level. Observe the immutable-binding diagnostic. Then mark the outer binding mutable and run again.

title: Functions and return values
summary: Pass values to a function, choose a return type, and call the function recursively.

sections.heading: Declare a function
sections.text: Parameters use name: type. The arrow introduces a return type. Give value-returning functions an explicit return type for a native build.

sections.heading: Return a result
sections.text: A final expression without a semicolon supplies the result of a block or function. An explicit return exits the current function even inside a nested block.

sections.heading: Follow the base case
sections.text: fibonacci returns n when n is smaller than two. Other inputs call the function twice with smaller arguments. Change the input to 7 and update the printed label. The result is 13.

sections.heading: Budget recursive work
sections.text: The interpreter allows 64 simultaneous calls. Its step budget also counts the many separate calls in this example. Use iteration for inputs that would require excessive recursion.

title: Conditions and loops
summary: Make a decision, update a loop variable, and exit with a result.

sections.heading: Test a condition
sections.text: if and while require booleans. The operators ==, !=, <, <=, > and >= compare values. Use && and || for short-circuit boolean expressions.

sections.heading: Move toward termination
sections.text: Each iteration of Euclid’s algorithm replaces the pair (x, y) with (y, x % y). For positive inputs the remainder gets smaller until y reaches zero.

sections.heading: Use loop, break and continue
sections.text: while checks a condition before every iteration. loop repeats until its body exits. break exits the nearest loop, and break value gives a loop expression a result. continue moves to the next iteration.

sections.heading: Try a change
sections.text: Run gcd(18, 48) and gcd(48, 0). The results are 6 and 48.

title: Numeric vectors
summary: Create a vector, read its length, index a value, and reduce it to a scalar.

sections.heading: Construct and read
sections.text: A literal such as [2.0, 4.0, 8.0] creates an immutable numeric vector. Values are stored as f64. len(v) returns an i64 count. at(v, i) returns the f64 at the zero-based integer index.

sections.heading: Sum and dot
sections.text: sum(v) adds the elements. dot(a, b) multiplies corresponding elements and adds the products. The two vectors must have equal lengths. Both reductions return f64.

sections.heading: Interpret the weighted mean
sections.text: The weighted total is 30 and the weights sum to 4. Dividing the first by the second gives 7.5. Replacing the weights with three ones gives 7.

sections.heading: Handle boundary cases
sections.text: Check that an index is at least zero and smaller than len(v) before calling at. Decide how to handle empty input and zero total weight before dividing.

title: Fit and evaluate a model
summary: Fit one coefficient from paired observations and use it to predict a new response.

sections.heading: Choose a model
sections.text: This example fits y = slope × x with the intercept fixed at zero. The four input observations and four targets appear directly in the program.

sections.heading: Fit one parameter
sections.text: dot(samples, targets) gives 60 and dot(samples, samples) gives 30. Their ratio minimizes the sum of squared residuals for this model. The denominator must be nonzero.

sections.heading: Predict on a new input
sections.text: The fitted slope is 2. Multiplying by an unseen input of 5 predicts 10. Change the targets to [3.0, 6.0, 9.0, 12.0]. The two outputs become 3 and 15.

sections.heading: Evaluate residuals
sections.text: The example library includes a separate mean squared error program and a two-feature threshold classifier. All three execute with the CPU vector operations in Blyx 0.2.0.

title: Project layout and CLI
summary: Create a project and check, run, or format the main source file.

sections.heading: Create a project
sections.text: new creates a directory with a Blyx.toml manifest and src/main.blyx. Run the command from the directory where you want the project to live.

sections.heading: Check syntax
sections.text: check reads a single source file and reports parser diagnostics. A successful syntax check can still be followed by a runtime error.

sections.heading: Execute the source
sections.text: run starts main in the interpreter. The generated starter prints Hello, Blyx!

sections.heading: Normalize line endings
sections.text: fmt normalizes the source file’s line endings in place. The separate blyxpkg tool is a prototype. Dependencies and registry publishing are outside the released CLI workflow.

title: Build a native executable
summary: Compile the synchronous, typed subset for the machine running the compiler.

sections.heading: Build the program
sections.text: Install rustc and a host linker. From your project directory, run the build command. By default the executable sits beside the source, with .exe on Windows.

sections.heading: Pick an output name
sections.text: On Linux or macOS, use the following commands to build and launch the executable.

sections.heading: Run on Windows
sections.text: From PowerShell, use an .exe output name and a relative path to start the file.

sections.heading: Keep types consistent
sections.text: Use typed parameters, explicit return types for functions that produce values, and matching scalar operand types. The native backend lowers supported Blyx syntax to Rust and invokes rustc. The produced executable runs without the compiler toolchain.

title: Understand diagnostics
summary: Distinguish syntax errors from runtime errors and control execution limits.

sections.heading: Read the first syntax error
sections.text: A parser diagnostic includes a line and column. Start at that location and check the preceding token, especially braces, parentheses and statement terminators.

sections.heading: Guard integer division
sections.text: In the example, && evaluates the right operand only if the divisor is nonzero. The first call prints false without dividing. The second call prints true.

sections.heading: Recognize runtime failures
sections.text: Integer overflow, division by zero, incompatible vector lengths and out-of-range indexing produce execution errors. In the CLI, run exits with status 4 for a runtime error.

sections.heading: Limit work
sections.text: The interpreter defaults to one million steps. You can give a terminating program a different budget with a positive integer. Browser runs also have an eight-second wall-clock limit.

title: Use Blyx in VS Code
summary: Run the current buffer and see parser feedback while typing.

sections.heading: Install the release
sections.text: Download blyx-language-1.2.0.vsix from the Blyx 0.2.0 GitHub release. In desktop VS Code, open Extensions, choose Install from VSIX, and select the file.

sections.heading: Run the current buffer
sections.text: Open a .blyx file or set the editor language to Blyx. Use Blyx: Run File in the Command Palette. The Blyx output channel shows the program’s output, including results from unsaved edits.

sections.heading: Read parser diagnostics
sections.text: The extension runs the bundled WebAssembly parser as you edit. Its interpreter works locally. A separate CLI installation is useful when you want a native executable.

title: Release capabilities
summary: Check which Blyx features you can use in 0.2.0 and where their limits lie.

sections.heading: Available in the interpreter
sections.text: Functions, lexical scopes, bindings, assignment, conditionals, while, loop, break, continue and print macros run today. Numeric operations include checked integers, f64 arithmetic, vector literals, len, at, sum and dot.

sections.heading: Native subset
sections.text: The build path supports synchronous, non-generic functions and the documented scalar and vector types. Type annotations affect native builds. The tree-walking interpreter performs runtime value-kind checks.

sections.heading: Under development
sections.text: Async execution, GPU kernels, actor scheduling, module imports, external packages, model serving, ownership checking and a general-purpose tensor runtime remain development work. Applications that depend on those features need another implementation path today.

sections.heading: Performance measurements
sections.text: The project publishes the source, raw sample timings and environment for its Fibonacci command-line benchmark. Comparing different workloads requires measuring them separately.
